welcome_lead: Stretch — analyse the structural methods top writers use across whole texts.
meta_desc: GCSE English Language stretch — focalisation, free indirect style, structural patterns, narrative shifts.
final_note: You explored focalisation, free indirect style, narrative shifts and zooming structural patterns.

concepts.def: Whose viewpoint we experience events through
Change in viewpoint, time or focus
Moving from wide view to small detail or vice versa
Opening in the middle of the action

walkthroughs.body_html: A child focaliser only sees fragments. A god-eye narrator sees all. The writer's choice limits — or expands — what we know.

3rd-person, but slipping into the character's mind: 'She hated him. How DARE he turn up like this.'

The italicised second sentence is HER voice — but in narration.

Writers zoom from wide ('the whole city slept') to narrow ('one light burned in one window'). It directs the reader's eye.

Then they pull back — and the meaning lands.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a dialect and an accent?
options: Dialect and accent mean the same thing.
Transitive verbs end in -ed and intransitive in -ing.
A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.
Accent refers only to pronunciation; dialect includes vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation — so all dialects involve accents but not vice versa.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between voiced and voiceless sounds?
options: Voiced sounds use the lips; voiceless sounds use the tongue.
Voiced sounds are loud and voiceless sounds are whispered.
Voiced sounds are produced with vocal-fold vibration (/b/, /d/, /g/, /z/); voiceless sounds without it (/p/, /t/, /k/, /s/). You can feel the difference by putting a hand on your throat.
A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between transitive and intransitive verbs?
options: Voiced sounds use the lips; voiceless sounds use the tongue.
Transitive verbs take a direct object ('she ate the cake'); intransitive verbs don't ('she slept'). Some verbs are both depending on use ('she ran' / 'she ran the company').
Transitive verbs are action verbs and intransitive are linking verbs.
Transitive verbs end in -ed and intransitive in -ing.
